# AI Policy

This chapter sets the rules for using AI in CWER work. The [AI Tools](ai-prompts.qmd) chapter that follows covers which tools we use and how to prompt them well. Read this one first.

The rules exist for three reasons. Participant data can leave Yale through a chat window and never come back. Funders and journals now impose specific requirements on AI use, and violating them puts our grants and publications at risk. And AI produces fluent, plausible, incorrect output, which threatens the credibility of the work we exist to produce.

## Scope

This policy applies to everyone working in CWER — faculty, staff, postdocs, graduate students, RAs, and collaborators — in any work carried out under CWER's name or with CWER data.

"AI" here means any system that generates text, code, images, or analysis in response to a prompt. That includes Claude, Gemini, Clarity, Consensus, NotebookLM, Grammarly, coding assistants in Cursor or Positron, transcription services, and any AI feature built into software we already use. The last category is the one people forget. Grammarly is an AI tool. A reference manager with a summarize button is an AI tool.

## The governing principle

**A human is accountable for every claim, number, citation, and line of code that leaves this lab.** AI assistance never transfers that accountability. It never excuses an error. It is never a defense.

This resolves most questions the policy does not explicitly address. If you could not defend an output to a reviewer who asked how you arrived at it, you do not submit it.

## Three questions to ask before you paste

### 1. What is the risk classification of this data?

Yale sorts data into low, moderate, and high risk ([definitions here](https://cybersecurity.yale.edu/data-classification)). Our participant data is high risk. Student education records from district partners are moderate risk under FERPA. Unpublished manuscripts, grant drafts, and internal reports are moderate risk. Published papers and public datasets are low risk.

If you are not sure, treat it as high risk and ask Mike or Joanna. This is the same rule we apply to storage, described in [Being a Team Member](../about/team-member.qmd), and for the same reason.

### 2. Does this data carry an external obligation?

Yale treats this as a **separate question** from risk classification, and for CWER it is the one that matters most. Our work runs through partnerships — PEER districts, school partners, agency collaborators — and most of that data arrives under a data use agreement. A DUA is a promise we made to someone else. Yale approving a platform does not amend that promise.

Yale states this on its own [Clarity security page](https://ai.yale.edu/yales-ai-tools-and-resources/clarity-platform/security): users with external obligations, such as data use agreements, must confirm that their use of Clarity is appropriate. It gives a concrete example — NIST 800-171 data cannot be used in Clarity at all, even though Clarity is otherwise cleared for high-risk data. NIST 800-171 compliance is what NIH controlled-access data requires. **If we hold NIH controlled-access data, it does not go into Clarity.**

Before any partner data goes into any AI tool, check the DUA and the IRB protocol. If they are silent, they do not permit it. Ask Mike or Joanna.

### 3. Even if you may, must you?

Yale's health sciences standards impose the **Minimum Necessary Principle**, and it applies no matter which platform you are using. Enter only what the task requires. Use de-identified or synthetic data whenever the task allows. Never submit direct identifiers unless they are essential. When unsure, leave it out.

This is the question people skip, and it is the cheapest protection available. Most of what we ask AI to do — critique an argument, tighten prose, debug an R function, explain a model — does not need the real data at all. A synthetic dataset with the same structure will do. Build one and paste that instead.

Note also that de-identification is harder than it looks. Yale's standards are strict and are not met by deleting names. An interview transcript that mentions a participant's job, neighborhood, and child's school is not de-identified.

## Which tool for which data

| Data | Tool |
|---|---|
| Identifiable or sensitive participant data | **Clarity only** — and only if the DUA and IRB protocol permit it |
| ePHI | **Clarity "Health" agents only** (agent names contain "Health"), only when essential, only under an approved IRB protocol, and only on a Yale-managed device. Requires an access request to `hsit-software@yale.edu`. Talk to Mike first. |
| **Internal** unpublished manuscripts, grant drafts, reports | Most models okay, but also see the judgment call below |
| **External** reviews of papers, grants, and reports | Assume forbidden unless you have confirmed otherwise in writing. Read journal and funder policies carefully — many bar AI use entirely. See below. |
| Published papers, public datasets, teaching material, your own non-confidential prose | Any approved tool, including Claude and Gemini |

Never paste real participant data into Claude, Gemini, Consensus, NotebookLM, Grammarly, or any tool outside Clarity. Use synthetic examples.

## The Clarity judgment call

Clarity is the most secure option available to us, but it is not the most capable.

Clarity gives us encrypted connections, no training on our inputs, coverage of most high-risk data, and a choice of models — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and others — at no cost. What it does not give us is the full feature set of the frontier products. It does not currently search the web or return live citations, which is why we use Consensus for evidence retrieval. Image generation is unavailable. Agent creation is limited and require approval. Chats are deleted after six months of inactivity, so do not treat it as an archive.

**For anything non-public, there is no tradeoff to weigh**, Claude and Gemini are simply not an option, so use Clarity. The judgment call exists only for low-risk work: public literature, teaching material, your own prose with nothing confidential in it. There, use the tool that does the job best. That is why the [AI Tools](ai-prompts.qmd) chapter still recommends Claude and Gemini for writing, reasoning, and code, and Consensus for literature.

When in doubt about which side of the line something falls on, ask. 

## Peer review

**Do not put any part of a manuscript or grant application you are reviewing into any AI tool, including Clarity, unless there is a policy stating otherwise or you have received written approval.** No summarizing. No "help me organize my critique." No pasting the abstract.

NIH prohibits reviewers from using large language models to analyze applications or formulate critiques ([NOT-OD-23-149](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-23-149.html)), and reviewers sign a confidentiality agreement certifying compliance. That prohibition is not conditioned on security, so a secure platform does not cure it. NSF prohibits uploading proposal content to non-approved AI tools. International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) holds that reviewer confidentiality may prohibit uploading a manuscript where confidentiality cannot be assured, and requires disclosure to the journal when AI is used in a review.

Sponsors that have published nothing specific about AI — IES, foundations, most agencies — still bind you through the confidentiality agreement you signed when you agreed to serve. The absence of an AI memo is not a loophole.

Two obligations are in play, and only one of them is about security. Confidentiality asks where the data went. Review integrity asks whose judgment the critique represents. The sponsor asked for yours.

**What you may do:** anything that never puts review content into the tool. Look up an unfamiliar method. Check a statistical assumption. Read into a literature the manuscript cites.

**If you want to do more,** email the program officer or editor before you start, describe exactly what you propose, and keep the written answer.

**If you have already done this,** tell Mike immediately. See "When something goes wrong" below. 

## Grant applications

For NIH receipt dates from September 25, 2025 forward, applications substantially developed by AI — in whole or in sections — are not considered the applicant's original ideas and will not be considered ([NOT-OD-25-132](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-25-132.html)). NIH also caps most PIs at six covered applications per calendar year, and states that AI-generated content detected after award may be referred to the Office of Research Integrity alongside enforcement actions up to termination.

**Permitted:** editing prose you wrote; formatting and compliance checks against the solicitation; drafting boilerplate administrative sections where the facts come from you and you verify every one; simulated critique of your own draft to find its weaknesses (see Mike's hitjob-grant tool as an example).

**Prohibited:** generating entire aims, significance, innovation, or approach as new text; generating a research strategy from a prompt describing your interests; producing entire data narratives you did not write.

The scientific argument, the aims, the design, and the claims originate with us. Note the asymmetry with the peer review section: running an AI critique against *our own* draft is encouraged, and running one against someone else's manuscript while you are their reviewer is prohibited. 

NSF encourages proposers to state in the project description whether and how generative AI was used. Check each sponsor's current terms every cycle since these rules are still evolving.

## Publication

**AI is never an author.** AI cannot take responsibility for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work, and responsibility is what authorship means.

**Disclose AI use at submission.** ICMJE directs journals to require disclosure of AI-assisted technologies used in producing the work, in both the cover letter and the manuscript, with writing assistance reported in the acknowledgments. COPE directs authors to disclose in the methods which tool was used and how, and its position covers writing, images, and the collection and analysis of data. Read the specific journal's instructions each time. **Nondisclosure may be construed as misconduct** — that is ICMJE's language, not ours.

Name the model, not just the platform. "Clarity" tells a reader nothing; Clarity routes to several different models, and which one produced the output is the fact a reader needs.

Draft language:

> The authors used [MODEL, e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.6, accessed via Yale's Clarity platform] to [edit prose for clarity and concision]. The authors reviewed and edited all content and take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

> [MODEL] was used to assist in drafting analysis code in R. All code was reviewed and validated by [NAME]. The authors take full responsibility for all analyses reported.

Two ICMJE rules that catch people: AI-generated material may not be cited as a primary source, and you must be able to assert there is no plagiarism in your paper, including in text the AI produced.

This is also why we **note AI contributions in script headers** — a practice already described in the [AI Tools](ai-prompts.qmd) chapter and consistent with the research integrity commitments in [Being a Team Member](../about/team-member.qmd).

## Verification

Nothing produced with AI assistance enters a deliverable until a human has checked it.

**Citations.** Open and read every reference an AI tool surfaces or formats. Not the abstract — the paper, to the extent your claim depends on it. Fabricated and subtly mis-attributed citations are the most common way AI use becomes a public embarrassment, and the error is invisible to anyone who does not check. This it's preferable to use Consensus, Google Scholar, or a database search for evidence retrieval rather than Claude or Gemini.

**Statistical code.** Review AI-assisted code line by line before it touches real data. Test it against a case with a known answer. Code that runs without error is not the same as code that is correct — a `-99` silently included in a mean produces a number, not a warning. Follow the quality control process in [Statistical Analysis](../analysis/statistical-analysis.qmd).

**Analytic output.** AI should not blindly choose the model specification, select covariates, or interpret results. A coefficient you did not derive is not a finding you can defend.

**Prose.** Read every sentence. If you would not say it, delete it. AI writing is fluent in a way that makes weak claims sound settled, and that fluency is the risk.

## Human subjects research

Our IRB protocols govern what we may do with participant data, and AI tools are third-party disclosures like any other. Clarity's security clearance does not amend a protocol.

Before any participant data--whether it's identifiable or de-identified--goes into any AI tool, confirm that the approved protocol and consent language permit it. If it's not in the protocol and you want to use AI, amend the protocol.

If an AI tool is part of a study design rather than a back-office aid, it belongs in the protocol explicitly: what the tool does, what participants are told, how outputs are validated, and what happens when the tool errs.

## Custom agents in Clarity

Clarity lets Yale faculty, staff, and sponsored students build [Custom Agents](https://ai.yale.edu/yales-ai-tools-and-resources/clarity-platform/custom-agents) at no cost. You can create own system prompt, a knowledge base of uploaded files, and control over who has access. Some constratints are that the model is fixed at creation and cannot be changed, each user gets five agents, group access is not self-service, and **ePHI is explicitly a non-suitable use case for Custom Agents**. Approval is tied to a specific use case, so repurposing an agent requires a new request.

Owners carry real obligations — access management, annual attestation, end-dating agents no longer in use, and notifying Yale if they leave. **Do not let a departing RA be the sole owner of an agent the lab depends on.** Talk to Mike before building one.

## When something goes wrong

People make mistakes with these tools. For example, someone will paste a manuscript under review into a chat window without thinking. Someone will submit a draft with a citation that does not exist. Someone will run partner data through Clarity because Clarity is "approved."

**Tell Mike or Joanna immediately.** Good-faith disclosure of an AI-related error is treated as exactly that: a correctable mistake, handled without penalty, and used to improve this policy. Concealment is a different matter and will be handled as a research integrity issue. Where the error involves a potential data incident, we contact the Yale Information Security Office.

## Keeping this current

This chapter is reviewed each June with the rest of the guide, and whenever NIH, NSF, our journals, or Yale issues new guidance. The underlying rules change faster than any policy document absorbs on its own. If you notice something out of date, tell Mike or Joanna.
